I'm 16, I've been telling stories for as long as I can remember, and I started putting them to paper three years ago. I've always been a "gifted" child--I excelled in math and science, and everyone told me how important and special I was because of my academic achievements, so I thought that my passion for writing was unimportant. I hid it. Even my parents and many of my closest friends had no idea I would pour hours and hours into my stories weekly, or even daily. This year, though, I took a high school writing class, which accompanied my English class. My teacher not only writes but is also very well-respected in the theater community, and has written several original pieces. It was only recently that I had the opportunity to write something creative for his class--a script for an original scene--and by the time I got around to it, I was exhausted from all of my academic work. I wrote the script in under two hours. It was far from my best work, but I simply didn't have the extra time to put into it. After I turned it in, my writing teacher approached me and told me it was outstanding, that he wished he'd had the opportunity to read my creative writing earlier, and that he wanted me to polish it and enter it in a short play contest next year. I'd hidden my love of writing for three years, and almost nobody had ever read, let alone praised, my work, so I was blown away--and I still am. I never dreamed that my "hobby" could be worth acknowledging, but now I was finally being told it was--not by the school system, but by a man who worked in a creative field. In the past few weeks I've opened up more and let more and more people read my work, again, outside of the school curriculum, and I've been told time and time again that I have a promising future in creative writing, if I choose to take it. I've been offered advice, I've been called a prodigy, people have offered to mentor me--it's astounding. And nothing I've shown people has been my best work! But I still have a hard time wrapping my mind around the idea that my creative achievements are more important than my academic ones...because only academic achievement is praised by the school system. I still have to sacrifice most of my time to math and science, because in the eyes of the school system, my writing is not worth a grade. In the eyes of the school system, my passion, my devotion to a creative outlet, means nothing.
I'm not the only person I know in this situation--my experience might be somewhat of an extreme case, but I know gifted artists and musicians who are also seeing their talent and creativity squandered by the school system. I've seen it at every school I've ever been to, with dozens and dozens of passionate people. I've witnessed the exact moment when people gave up on their dreams because they were told math and science were more important than what they loved. The school system kills creativity.

One of the biggest things I took out of it was
that I felt like he was trying to get across the point that everyone is
creative, but you’re not allowed to be creative in academics. He made the point
that schools prepare children to be college professors RATHER than to help them
be creative, as though a professor must be exempt from being able to have
original ideas. He also made the joke that during a social interaction,
academics are praying for it to end so that they can “go write a paper about it,”
as if to devalue talking about things in a structured way as a viable outlet of
expression. All throughout school, I was one of the few kids that valued
academics above everything else. When somebody asked me, “what’s your hobby?”
and I responded “doing math or learning about physics” people would respond,
“but what do you like to do for fun?” I’d have to give the answer “I play the
piano” instead because it’s a more acceptable answer as a leisure activity. But
I could do math the way a “normal” person my age played sports or played video
games. I could sit down and solve problem after problem for hours, or rearrange
problems and make my own in order to give myself a better understanding of a
mathematical concept. And then I could apply that concept to a physical
situation to find links between things in the real world that I never would
have realized otherwise. I don’t consider myself good at either math or
physics. Were I to ever achieve great success in the fields I would not want my
achievements to precede me the same way high achievers in the arts often seem
to. I would not want my achievements to precede me because I believe that I am
not good at the topics, I merely enjoy them, and I wouldn’t want someone to
feel like I was better than them just because I enjoyed something they didn’t.
Most, if not all people can do math faster than me. I am extremely slow at
doing my work, and for most of my life I felt like that was supposed to mean
that I wasn’t good at it. Eventually, I even grew to hate mathematics. However, at the height of my loathing in the 10th grade, I discovered that if
I tried hard enough, I could comprehend graduate level texts. I was impressed
with myself for this, and unlike the other things in life that I had wanted to
be good at in order to impress others (which admittedly is why I started doing
more complicated mathematics at first), I could do something that I myself
could be proud of, and I realized that was all that mattered. I derived great
joy from discovering new ideas and the ways they link together, or finding my
own new ways to understand something. I have even been brought to tears by the
beauty I find in mathematics, as silly as that may sound. I would even argue,
physics and mathematics are fields that praise creative individuals, as some of
the most notable physicists in history include the likes of Albert Einstein and
Richard Feynman, two men who revolutionized physics by working on ideas that
everyone had worked on before, but in entirely new ways. So, I'd that no, he is wrong. Schools could certainly be reworked to be more inclusive of children that like to do things like dance, sing, paint, etc., or just be more accepting of students that enjoy different
things and learn in different ways in general, but for some, the academic areas
in school are the places THEY get to show off their creativity, and in a world
that continues to attempt to be more inclusive of those we think are being
ignored, we must refrain ourselves from putting the kids we commonly see as
“uncreative” or “creative in the wrong ways” on the back burner, in favor of
those that we think are being ignored.

Do schools kill creativity? | Sir Ken Robinson 
 Throughout the speech, Sir Ken Robinson mainly discusses that schools suppress children's creativity. Schools today tend to treat mistakes as an unforgivable fault, as we can see teachers who go furious when we choose the wrong answer by mistake. Mistakes don't precisely signify creativity, but most revolutionary advances have derived from creative ideas thought to be a 'mistake' in that society. As schools make children fear making mistakes, they grow up to lose the ability to create something inventive and ingenious. Moreover, this phenomenon is occurring throughout the whole world. Schools kill children's creativity not only by prohibiting mistakes but by underestimating subjects regarding creativity so as art and dance. The speaker claims that this phenomenon occurs throughout the whole world since most countries consider the ultimate goal of public education is training professors, which requires not creativity but logic. Likewise, creativity is underrated since it is not essential in industrialized society. What jobs require defines people's value. Artists and musicians make less money, so they are less needed. Following society's common demand of intelligence, university naturally changed into the job training center. The presenter strongly argues that this view on education should be viewed differently. For example, ADHD is defined as an attention disorder, yet if we change our attitude toward it, we can find that people with ADHD are talented in bodily activities such as dancing. In conclusion, the author asserts that humans' future depends on whether they adjust their new concept of the education system which can lead to the flourishing of humanity.
 Even if the presentation was taken more than ten years ago, his idea is determined to be true. Also, the problem he mentioned is still not settled in Korea. What estimates people's value is the university and the specialty they majored in. Korea has not adapted to the fourth industrial revolution, concerned with computing technology that needs creativity. Exams in schools are taken not to give students motivation to study but to exclude them from success. Students in Korea are not "studying" but "memorizing" technical terms that they never understand. How could they make software and A.I.s though they have never created something new throughout their whole life? It is essential to reconsider the nature of the study.

Here's my conclusion. She didn't say this outright so I'll try to put together the pieces myself. Being vulnerable is extremely important in being connected (with others and without ourselves). How? By defeating shame, which is this fear of disconnection (hide this because if ppl knew they wouldn't like me). How? The research shows if you want this to be "easy" (i.e. to do this being a 'whole hearted' person) then you need to believe you are worthy of love and belonging.

This is hard. But we can break it down a bit. These ppl had: 
- courage. To be imperfect.
- compassion - to be kind to themselves first, then to others
- connection - as a result of authenticity (letting go of who you should be to embrace you you ARE.) 

This is not easy and requires a lot of personal work, speaking from experience. But in a nutshell, this is you accepting and tolerating yourself (by having empathy for what you went through as a kid) and therefore also learning to tolerate others. And in the realm of compassion, learning this teaches you to accept yourself and like yourself, leading to a sense of yes, you are worthy of love. And this makes you unafraid of being who you really are - with all your imperfections included, leading to no or minimal shame, leading to being vulnerable (and this being easy). 

Hope this helps!

Bill Gates’ TED talk on epidemic preparedness delivers an urgent message: the greatest risk of a global catastrophe is not war, but an infectious virus, that could kill millions. His analysis of the 2014 Ebola outbreak exposes critical gaps in global readiness and highlights how unprepared the world still is for the next pandemic, despite advances in science and technology.
Gates stresses that the failure to prepare adequately, such as insufficient global health infrastructure and poor coordination, could make the next epidemic far worse. The current tools and biological knowledge exist, but they must be integrated into a global health system. This includes strengthening health systems in poorer countries where outbreaks often begin, pairing medical teams with military logistics for rapid response, conducting realistic simulations and scenario planning, accelerating research and development for vaccines and treatments, etc.
Gates’ message is clear: “There’s no need to panic… but we need to get going”, since the cost of prevention is modest compared to the potential human and economic burden of a global pandemic. This talk challenges us to critically examine why, despite repeated warnings and scientific advances, global preparedness remains inadequate. It raises questions about political will, funding priorities and international cooperation. It also hints a reflection on individual and societal responsibilities in supporting public health measures. His TED talk is a crucial contribution to the discourse on global health security. It emphasizes that the next global catastrophe is likely to be a viral epidemic, most probably influenza, and without decisive action, the consequences could be devastating. Preparing now, using lessons from Ebola and current scientific insights about influenza, is not optional, but imperative.

I havent even gotten out of car yet, and she jumps on bicycle to greet me, and when she pulls up I notice both her tires are flat,  What the Hell,, come with me, and in the barn is airtank, and she cant believe how nice it is. Smiling at every crank of pedals... 

So I get request to weld up the cracked engine block on the tractor, And gather tools to remove items, and just about dark, she climbs up sitting on top of tractor, and cant wait to hold Flashlight to assist like any nurse during operation. 

Later, having diner, she'd climb up in my lap for a Fav'd book story and we both fall asleep after a long day. 
And a tough day by morning, rushing 55 miles to the airport to service airliner fleet of L-1011's for another round trip for 350 people back to Mpls Mn. 

Then I just get home and get a call shes just been killed running across the road to the little country store to save her dog.
